## 1 Overview

In this hands-on exercise, we will learn how to analyse and visualise text data using R.

By the end of this hands-on exercise, we will be able to:

* Understand the tidytext framework for processing, analysing, and visualising text data.
* Write functions to import multiple files into R.
* Merge multiple files into a single data frame.
* Clean and wrangle text data using the tidyverse approach.
* Create word clouds to visualise prominent terms.
* Compute Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) using the tidytext methodology.
* Visualise relationships among texts and terms.

## 2 Getting Started

In this hands-on lab, you will learn to manage, process, clean, analyze, and visualize textual data using the following R libraries:

* **Core Text & Data Wrangling**: tidytext, tidyverse (readr, purrr, stringr, ggplot2), lubridate, and hms

* **Text Relationships & Tables**: widyr and DT

* **Visualization & Graphing**: wordcloud, ggwordcloud, and textplot (along with its dependencies: igraph, tidygraph, and ggraph)

:::: {.panel-tabset}

### (a) Install Libraries

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

pacman::p_load(tidytext, widyr, wordcloud, DT, ggwordcloud, textplot, lubridate, hms, tidyverse, tidygraph, ggraph, igraph)
```

### (b) Import data

#### (i) Creating a folder list

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

news20 <- "data/20news/"
```

#### (ii) Reading all files from a folder

As there are many files in the folder, we shall first create a function to read all the files from a folder into a dataframe.

::: {.panel-tabset}

##### Step 1: Create a function to read all files

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder, 
                    full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file, 
                      read_lines)) %>%
    transmute(id = basename(file), 
              text) %>%
    unnest(text)
}
```

##### Step 2: Importing all messages

Next, we implement the function and read in all the files in the folder.
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

raw_text <- tibble(folder = 
                     dir(news20, 
                         full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder, 
                          read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  transmute(newsgroup = basename(folder), 
            id, text)

dir.create("data/rds", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_rds(raw_text, "data/rds/news20.rds")
```

::: callout-note
![](images/transparent_right_andy.png){width="120px"}[Points to Note]{style="font-size:30px; font-weight:bold;"}

* [read_lines()](https://readr.tidyverse.org/reference/read_lines.html) of readr package is used to read up to n_max lines from a file.
* [map()](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/reference/map.html) of purrr package is used to transform their input by applying a function to each element of a list and returning an object of the same length as the input.
* [unnest()](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/nest.html) of dplyr package is used to flatten a list-column of data frames back out into regular columns.
* [mutate()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate.html) of dplyr is used to add new variables and preserves existing ones;
* [transmute()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/transmute.html) of dplyr is used to add new variables and drops existing ones.
* [read_rds()](https://readr.tidyverse.org/reference/read_rds.html) is used to save the extracted and combined data frame as rds file for future use.

:::


##### Step 3: Initial EDA

Figure below shows the frequency of messages by newsgroup.

```{r}
library(patchwork)

## sort by number of messages
p1 <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  summarize(messages = n_distinct(id)) %>%
  mutate(newsgroup = reorder(newsgroup, messages)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(messages, newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen") +
  labs(y = NULL)

## show word count
p2 <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  summarize(words = n()) %>%
  mutate(newsgroup = reorder(newsgroup, words)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(words, newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen") +
  labs(y = NULL, x = "word count")

p1 + p2
```

:::

::::

## 3 Introducing tidytext

* Using tidy data principles in processing, analysing and visualising text data.
* Much of the infrastructure needed for text mining with tidy data frames already exists in packages like ‘dplyr’, ‘broom’, ‘tidyr’, and ‘ggplot2’.

:::: {.panel-tabset}

### (a) Removing headers and automated email signatures
* Irrelevant Text: Every message contains structural elements and extra text that need to be excluded from the analysis.
* Header Metadata: Each message has a header with descriptive fields (such as "from:" or "in_reply_to:") that should be filtered out.
* Email Signatures: Automated signatures are often present at the bottom of the messages.
* Signature Marker: These signatures can be identified because they appear directly after a standard delimiter line ("--").

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(cumsum(text == "") > 0,
         cumsum(str_detect(
           text, "^--")) == 0) %>%
  ungroup()
```

::: callout-note
![](images/transparent_left_andy.png){width="120px"}[Points to Note]{style="font-size:30px; font-weight:bold;"}

* [cumsum()](https://rdrr.io/r/base/cumsum.html) of base R is used to return a vector whose elements are the cumulative sums of the elements of the argument.
* [str_detect()](https://stringr.tidyverse.org/reference/str_detect.html) from stringr is used to detect the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.

:::

### (b) Removing lines with quotes

In this code chunk below, regular expressions are used to remove with nested text representing quotes from other users.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]")
         | text == "",
         !str_detect(text, 
                     "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
         !str_detect(text, 
                     "^In article <")
  )
```

::: callout-note
![](images/transparent_left_andy.png){width="120px"}[Points to Note]{style="font-size:30px; font-weight:bold;"}

* [str_detect()](https://stringr.tidyverse.org/reference/str_detect.html) from **stringr** is used to detect the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.
* [filter()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/filter.html) of **dplyr** package is used to subset a data frame, retaining all rows that satisfy the specified conditions.

:::

### (c) Textual Data processing

In this code chunk below, [unnest_tokens()](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/tidytext/versions/0.3.1/topics/unnest_tokens) of **tidytext** package is used to split the dataset into tokens, while [stop_words()](https://rdrr.io/cran/tidytext/man/stop_words.html) is used to remove stop-words.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z']$"),
         !word %in% stop_words$word)
```

Now that we’ve removed the headers, signatures, and formatting, we can start exploring common words. For starters, we could find the most common words in the entire dataset, or within particular newsgroups.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

usenet_words %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)
```

Instead of counting individual word, we can also count words within by newsgroup by using the code chunk below.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

words_by_newsgroup <- usenet_words %>%
  count(newsgroup, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup()
```

### (d) Word Clouds

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### (i) basic word cloud

In this code chunk below, `wordcloud()` of **wordcloud package** is used to plot a static wordcloud, including a data table for information discovery.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

wordcloud(words_by_newsgroup$word,
          words_by_newsgroup$n,
          max.words = 300)

# Interactive data table
datatable(words_by_newsgroup,
          filter = "top",
          options = list(pageLength = 10,
                         scrollX = TRUE))
```



#### (ii) ggwordcloud

The wordcloud below is plotted by using [ggwordcloud](https://lepennec.github.io/ggwordcloud/) package.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

set.seed(1234)

words_by_newsgroup %>%
  filter(n > 0) %>%
ggplot(aes(label = word,
           size = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  theme_minimal() +
  facet_wrap(~newsgroup)
```

:::

::::

## 4 Basic Concept of TF-IDF

* [tf–idf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tf%E2%80%93idf), short for term frequency–inverse document frequency, is a numerical statistic that is intended to reflect how important a word is to a document in a collection of [corpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text_corpus).

$$
idf(\text{term}) = \ln \left( \frac{n_{\text{documents}}}{n_{\text{documents containing term}}} \right)
$$

:::: {.panel-tabset}

### (a) computing TF-IDF

The code chunk below uses bind_tf_idf() of tidytext to compute and bind the term frequency, inverse document frequency and ti-idf of a tidy text dataset to the dataset.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

tf_idf <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, newsgroup, n) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))
```

### (b) interactive table

Table below is an interactive table created by using `datatable()`. This is created using the below code chunk that creates a html table that allows pagination of rows and columns.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

DT::datatable(tf_idf, filter = 'top') %>% 
  formatRound(columns = c('tf', 'idf', 
                          'tf_idf'), 
              digits = 3) %>%
  formatStyle(0, 
              target = 'row', 
              lineHeight='25%')
```

::: callout-note
![](images/transparent_left_andy.png){width="120px"}[Points to Note]{style="font-size:30px; font-weight:bold;"}

* `filter()` argument is used to turn control the filter UI.
* `formatRound()` is used to customise the values format. The argument digits define the number of decimal places.
* `formatStyle()` is used to customise the output table. In this example, the arguments target and lineHeight are used to reduce the line height by 25%.

:::


### (c) facted bar charts

Facet bar charts technique is used to visualise the tf-idf values of science related newsgroup.

```{r}
tf_idf %>%
  filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, 
            n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, 
                        tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf, 
             word, 
             fill = newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ newsgroup, 
             scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "tf-idf", 
       y = NULL)
```


::::


## 5 Counting and Correlating Pairs of Words

* **Goal**: Calculate how often two words appear together in the same document (pairwise counts) or determine their correlation.

* **The Matrix Problem**: Most tools require reshaping tidy data into a wide matrix to perform these pairwise calculations.

* **The widyr Solution**: The [widyr](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/widyr/index.html) package streamlines this workflow behind the scenes by temporarily casting tidy data into a wide matrix, running the operation (like correlation), and immediately re-tidying the results.


:::: {.panel-tabset}

### (a) widyr package

In this code chunk below, pairwise_cor() of widyr package is used to compute the correlation between newsgroup based on the common words found.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

newsgroup_cors <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  pairwise_cor(newsgroup, 
               word, 
               n, 
               sort = TRUE)
```

### (b) visualising correlation

We can visualise the relationship between newgroups in network graph as shown below.

```{r}
set.seed(2017)

newsgroup_cors %>%
  filter(correlation > .025) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame() %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = correlation, 
                     width = correlation)) +
  geom_node_point(size = 6, 
                  color = "lightblue") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 color = "red",
                 repel = TRUE) +
  theme_void()
```

### (c) n-grams

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### (i) creating n-grams

In this code chunk below, a bigram and trigram data frames are created by using `unnest_tokens()` of tidytext.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

bigrams <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram, 
                text, 
                token = "ngrams", 
                n = 2)

trigrams <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(trigram, 
                text, 
                token = "ngrams", 
                n = 3)

bigrams

trigrams
```

#### (ii) counting n-grams

We can count and sort the bigram and trigram data frames in ascending order.

##### without stop words filtering
```{r}
bigrams_count <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != 'NA') %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(!str_detect(word1, "^[0-9]+$"),
         !str_detect(word2, "^[0-9]+$")) %>%
  count(bigram = paste(word1, word2), sort = TRUE)

trigrams_count <- trigrams %>%
  filter(trigram != 'NA') %>%
  separate(trigram, c("word1", "word2", "word3"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(!str_detect(word1, "^[0-9]+$"),
         !str_detect(word2, "^[0-9]+$"),
         !str_detect(word3, "^[0-9]+$")) %>%
  count(trigram = paste(word1, word2, word3), sort = TRUE)

bigrams_count
trigrams_count

```


##### with stop words filerting
```{r}
bigrams_count <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != 'NA') %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word,
         !word2 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!str_detect(word1, "^[0-9]+$"),
         !str_detect(word2, "^[0-9]+$")) %>%
  count(bigram = paste(word1, word2), sort = TRUE)

trigrams_count <- trigrams %>%
  filter(trigram != 'NA') %>%
  separate(trigram, c("word1", "word2", "word3"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word,
         !word2 %in% stop_words$word,
         !word3 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!str_detect(word1, "^[0-9]+$"),
         !str_detect(word2, "^[0-9]+$"),
         !str_detect(word3, "^[0-9]+$")) %>%
  count(trigram = paste(word1, word2, word3), sort = TRUE)
bigrams_count
trigrams_count

```

#### (iii) network graphs of n-grams

The ggraph package is used to plot the bigram and trigram.

##### the chart below has no stop words filtering
```{r}
library(igraph)
library(ggraph)
library(patchwork)

# Add these at the top of the unfiltered chunk
set.seed(1234)
a <- grid::arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(.15, "inches"))

# Build unfiltered graphs
bigram_graph_unfiltered <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != 'NA') %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  count(bigram = paste(word1, word2), sort = TRUE) %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(n > 20) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame()

trigram_graph_unfiltered <- trigrams %>%
  filter(trigram != 'NA') %>%
  separate(trigram, c("word1", "word2", "word3"), sep = " ") %>%
  count(trigram = paste(word1, word2, word3), sort = TRUE) %>%
  separate(trigram, c("word1", "word2", "word3"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(n > 3) %>%   # lower threshold
  graph_from_data_frame()

# Plot
p3 <- ggraph(bigram_graph_unfiltered, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n),
                 show.legend = FALSE,
                 arrow = a,
                 end_cap = circle(.07, 'inches')) +
  geom_node_point(color = "lightblue", size = 5) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), vjust = 1, hjust = 1) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Bigram Network (Unfiltered)")

p4 <- ggraph(trigram_graph_unfiltered, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n),
                 show.legend = FALSE,
                 arrow = a,
                 end_cap = circle(.07, 'inches')) +
  geom_node_point(color = "lightblue", size = 5) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), vjust = 1, hjust = 1) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Trigram Network (Unfiltered)")

p3 + p4

```


##### the chart below has stop words filtered off
```{r}
set.seed(1234)
a <- grid::arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(.15, "inches"))

# Build graphs
bigram_graph <- bigrams_count %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(n > 3) %>%   # lower threshold
  graph_from_data_frame()

trigram_graph <- trigrams_count %>%
  separate(trigram, c("word1", "word2", "word3"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(n > 1) %>%   # lower threshold
  graph_from_data_frame()

# Plot
p1 <- ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n),
                 show.legend = FALSE,
                 arrow = a,
                 end_cap = circle(.07, 'inches')) +
  geom_node_point(color = "lightblue", size = 5) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), vjust = 1, hjust = 1) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Bigram Network")

p2 <- ggraph(trigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n),
                 show.legend = FALSE,
                 arrow = a,
                 end_cap = circle(.07, 'inches')) +
  geom_node_point(color = "lightblue", size = 5) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), vjust = 1, hjust = 1) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Trigram Network")

p1 + p2
```
